title: Acute Stress Orthomolecular Nutrition (ASON): A Systems-Medicine Hypothesis and Framework for Dynamic Nutrient Requirements
content: Acute stress can change metabolism, immune activity, redox regulation, microcirculation, nutrient distribution, tissue repair, and the interaction among these systems. These changes raise the possibility that the functional availability or requirement for selected nutrients differs temporarily from that during physiological maintenance. Acute Stress Orthomolecular Nutrition (ASON) is proposed as a systems-medicine hypothesis and research framework for investigating this possibility across infection, including COVID-19; surgery, including dental procedures; trauma and burns; ischemic cardiovascular and cerebrovascular injury; intense physical exertion and recovery; and, more provisionally, acute neuroendocrine or psychological stress.The framework distinguishes altered circulating concentration, altered turnover or loss, functional nutrient limitation, and clinical benefit from intervention. None establishes the next automatically. ASON further treats nutrient physiology as one component of a changing biological terrain in which metabolic state, inflammatory burden, redox signaling, microcirculation, organ function, baseline nutritional status, environmental exposures, and repair capacity may interact. Selected perioperative nutritional strategies provide clinical precedents, but uncertainty in systematic reviews and null or harmful results in critical illness impose substantial boundaries. ASON neither predicts uniformly increased requirements nor supports universal high-dose supplementation. Nutrient effects must be evaluated according to baseline status, stressor, disease severity, organ function, formulation, dose, route, timing, and duration.This narrative framework proposes serial systems-level physiological measurements followed by prespecified, adequately controlled intervention studies with patient-centered outcomes and adverse-event monitoring. Its incremental value would depend on demonstrating reproducible stress-related changes, identifying functionally relevant limitations, and, separately, showing that targeted interventions improve outcomes safely. Acute psychological stress remains a hypothesis-generating extension without an established acute nutrient-treatment indication.
